title: Properties of layer normalization
prompt: Which statements about layer normalization are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In layer normalization, gamma and beta are learned per feature dimension.
options.explanation: After normalizing a sample's feature vector, LayerNorm applies a learnable scale gamma and shift beta. Both are vectors with one entry per feature dimension, so the layer can recover any scale and offset it needs.

options.text: It requires running mean and variance estimates at test time.
options.explanation: LayerNorm computes the mean and variance of each sample over its own features, so there is nothing to estimate across the dataset and no running statistics are stored. Running averages belong to BatchNorm, which is why the two are often confused.

options.text: Layer normalization requires a large batch to be effective.
options.explanation: The statistics come from the features of one sample, so the result does not depend on the batch size at all and LayerNorm works with a batch of 1. A large batch is what BatchNorm needs to get stable batch statistics.

options.text: It uses the same normalization rule during training and evaluation.
options.explanation: Because the statistics are always computed from the current sample, there is no batch statistic or running average that could differ between modes. Training and evaluation therefore apply exactly the same computation.

hints: Ask over which axis the mean and variance are computed: the samples of a batch or the features of one sample?
If the statistics never involve other samples, is there anything left to store for test time?
explanation: LayerNorm normalizes each sample over its own feature dimensions and then applies a learnable per-feature scale (gamma) and shift (beta). Since it never looks at other samples, it needs no batch, keeps no running statistics and behaves identically in training and evaluation. These are exactly the properties that distinguish it from BatchNorm, which normalizes over the batch, needs reasonably large batches and switches to running averages at test time.

title: Batch normalization at inference
prompt: Which of the following statements about batch normalization during inference are correct? Assume the model is in evaluation mode and batch normalization uses its default settings. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The shift and rescale step is skipped at test time.
options.explanation: The learned scale gamma and shift beta are ordinary parameters and are applied in evaluation mode too. Only the source of the mean and variance changes at test time (running estimates instead of batch statistics).

options.text: Batch normalization requires a test batch to contain at least two examples.
options.explanation: In evaluation mode the stored running mean and variance are used, so a single example is enough. The two-example restriction applies to training mode, where a variance has to be computed from the batch.

options.text: At inference, the mean and variance are exponential moving averages of the values seen during training.
options.explanation: During training the layer updates running_mean and running_var after every batch with an exponential moving average (default momentum 0.1). These stored values replace the batch statistics in evaluation mode.

options.text: During testing, batch normalization is a fixed affine transformation (scaling and shifting).
options.explanation: With the running mean mu, running variance sigma squared, gamma and beta all fixed, the output is gamma*(x - mu)/sqrt(sigma^2 + eps) + beta, i.e. a per-channel scale and shift of the input.

hints: Which statistics does BatchNorm use in train mode and which in eval mode?
Which quantities are fixed at test time, and what kind of function of x do you get when mu, sigma, gamma and beta are all constants?
explanation: In training BatchNorm normalizes with the statistics of the current batch and updates exponential moving averages of the mean and variance. In evaluation mode it uses these stored averages together with the learned gamma and beta, so every input is processed independently by the same per-channel affine map. That is why batch size at test time is irrelevant and why the shift and rescale step is not skipped.

title: Properties of self-attention
prompt: A self-attention layer receives $P$ input vectors $X \in \mathbb{R}^{P\times D}$ (no positional encoding). It computes $Q = XW_Q$, $K = XW_K$, $V = XW_V$, the attention weights $A = \text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{D})$ with the softmax taken over each row, and the outputs $Y = AV$. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: $A$ has shape $P \times P$, and every row of $A$ sums to 1.
options.explanation: $QK^\top$ has one row per query and one column per key, giving $P\times P$ scores. The softmax is applied along each row, so every row becomes a probability distribution over the keys and sums to 1.

options.text: $A$ is symmetric, because the queries and the keys are computed from the same input vectors.
options.explanation: Queries and keys use different matrices $W_Q$ and $W_K$, so in general $Q_i\cdot K_j \neq Q_j\cdot K_i$. Even with symmetric scores, the row-wise softmax divides each row by a different normalizer and would break the symmetry. Using the same inputs does not make the projections equal.

options.text: Each output vector $Y_i$ depends only on its own input vector $X_i$.
options.explanation: $Y_i = \sum_j A_{i,j} V_j$ is a weighted mix of the value vectors of all inputs, with weights depending on all keys. Self-attention is precisely the sub-layer in which the vectors interact; the per-vector independence is a property of the MLP.

options.text: Permuting the input vectors permutes the output vectors in the same way.
options.explanation: Without positional encoding, self-attention is permutation equivariant: reordering the rows of $X$ reorders the rows and columns of $A$ and the rows of $Y$ consistently, so $f(s(x)) = s(f(x))$. This is why position information has to be added explicitly.

hints: Write out what the entry $(i, j)$ of $QK^\top$ is and whether swapping $i$ and $j$ gives the same number.
Does the formula for $Y_i$ involve only $X_i$, or all rows of $X$?
explanation: The attention matrix $A$ has one row per query and one column per key; each row is a softmax over the keys, so rows sum to 1 (but columns need not). $A$ is not symmetric because different projections $W_Q$ and $W_K$ are used. Every output is a convex combination of all value vectors, so tokens interact only inside attention. Since nothing in the layer depends on the order of the inputs, it is permutation equivariant, which is why positional encodings are needed to inject order.

title: Pre-norm versus post-norm transformer blocks
prompt: Two transformer blocks act on tokens x of shape (N, P, D), where attn is a self-attention layer and mlp a two-layer MLP applied to each token. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
code:
# post-norm
x = norm1(x + attn(x))
x = norm2(x + mlp(x))

# pre-norm
x = x + attn(norm1(x))
x = x + mlp(norm2(x))

options.text: In the pre-norm block, the input x reaches the output through the residual connections without passing through any LayerNorm.
options.explanation: In the pre-norm block the LayerNorms sit inside the residual branches (norm1 and norm2 only normalize the input of the sub-layer). The skip path x + ... is untouched, so the identity route from input to output contains no normalization.

options.text: The MLP is the sub-layer in which the P tokens exchange information with each other.
options.explanation: The MLP is applied to every token separately with the same weights. Only attention mixes information across tokens, so the claim confuses the two sub-layers.

options.text: If the output projection of attn and the last linear layer of mlp are initialised to zero (weights and biases), the pre-norm block computes the identity at initialisation.
options.explanation: With zero final weights and biases both sub-layers output exactly 0, whatever their normalized input is. The block then returns x + 0 + 0 = x.

options.text: With the same zero initialisation, the post-norm block also computes the identity at initialisation.
options.explanation: Both sub-layers still output 0, but the block then returns norm2(norm1(x)). The LayerNorms sit on the residual path and re-normalize every token (zero mean, unit variance per token), which changes x unless it was already normalized.

hints: Look at where norm1 and norm2 sit relative to the addition x + ... in each block.
If a sub-layer outputs exactly 0, what is left of each line of the block?
explanation: The difference between the blocks is the position of LayerNorm. In pre-norm it is applied to the input of each sub-layer, leaving a clean residual path from input to output, so zeroing the last layer of each sub-layer gives exactly the identity. In post-norm it is applied after the addition, so every token is re-normalized even when the sub-layers contribute nothing. Token mixing happens only in attention; the MLP works per token.

title: BatchNorm2d after a conv-ReLU-pool stack
prompt: The input x has shape (N, 32, 16, 16). The convolution uses stride 1 and the pooling halves the spatial size. Find the missing num_features of the BatchNorm2d layer, then count the trainable parameters of bn alone (affine=True; running statistics are not trainable).
code:
import torch.nn as nn

layers = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)
)
features = layers(x)
bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(____, affine=True)
y = bn(features)
hints: Follow the shape of x through the convolution, ReLU and pooling. Which dimension does BatchNorm2d care about?
With affine=True, how many learnable numbers does BatchNorm keep per channel?
explanation:
Shapes: the 3x3 convolution with padding 1 keeps the spatial size and produces 64 channels, giving (N, 64, 16, 16); ReLU keeps the shape; max-pooling 2x2 with stride 2 gives (N, 64, 8, 8). num_features is the channel count C of an (N, C, H, W) input, so it is 64.

Parameters: BatchNorm learns one scale (gamma) and one bias (beta) per channel, 64 + 64 = 128. The running mean and running variance are buffers, not trainable parameters, and neither the batch size nor the spatial size changes the count.

Typical wrong results: 32 (input channels instead of output channels), 4096 (64*8*8, counting every feature-map position), 256 (counting the 128 running statistics as trainable, or 2*128 from a 128-channel layer), 64 (only the scales, forgetting the biases).

title: Attention weights and parameters of a bottleneck attention layer
prompt:
The U-Net bottleneck x has shape (N, 128, 8, 8). It is turned into tokens (one token per spatial position, the channels as features) and passed through a self-attention layer with a fused qkv projection and an output projection, both with biases.

(a) The attention weights are computed for every image of the batch, so their shape is (N, P, P). Give P.

(b) How many trainable parameters does attn have?
code:
import torch.nn as nn

class SelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(dim, 3 * dim)   # queries, keys and values
        self.proj = nn.Linear(dim, dim)      # output projection

tokens = x.flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)        # (N, P, D)
attn = SelfAttention(128)
y = attn(tokens)
hints: x.flatten(2) merges the two spatial dimensions. How many positions does an 8x8 map have?
Count each nn.Linear as in_features*out_features + out_features, and note that the number of tokens does not enter the parameter count.
explanation:
(a) flatten(2) merges the 8x8 spatial positions into P = 64 tokens and transpose(1, 2) puts the 128 channels last, so tokens has shape (N, 64, 128) with D = 128. Every token attends to every token, so there is one 64x64 attention matrix per image: shape (N, 64, 64), hence P = 64.

(b) qkv: 128*384 + 384 = 49,152 + 384 = 49,536. proj: 128*128 + 128 = 16,384 + 128 = 16,512. Total 49,536 + 16,512 = 66,048 (= 4*128^2 + 4*128).

Typical wrong results: 65,536 (forgetting the biases), 49,536 (counting only qkv), 16,512 (counting only proj), 128 for (a) (confusing the token dimension D with the number of tokens) and 4096 for (a) (flattening the P x P matrix). The parameter count never depends on P or on the batch size.

title: Optimizer factory: SGD branch
description: Builds an optimizer by name. The function first creates parameter groups that already carry the weight-decay settings, then returns the optimizer matching the requested name using the given learning rate and momentum.
code:
import torch
import torch.optim as optim

def make_optimizer(model, name, lr, weight_decay=5e-4, momentum=0.9):
    # make_parameter_groups is assumed to be defined
    params = make_parameter_groups(model, weight_decay)
    name = name.lower()

    if name == "sgd":
        return <<BLANK:sgd>>

    raise ValueError(f"Unknown optimizer: {name}")
hints: The optimizer classes live in torch.optim, which is imported as optim.
The first argument is not model.parameters() here: the parameter groups were already built. Which other two function arguments belong to SGD?
explanation: optim.SGD(params, lr=lr, momentum=momentum) passes the pre-built parameter groups (which already contain the per-group weight_decay), the learning rate and the momentum coefficient. Passing model.parameters() would ignore the groups and their weight-decay settings; omitting momentum would silently fall back to plain SGD with momentum 0; adding weight_decay again is unnecessary because it is set inside the groups.

title: Residual connection in a basic block
description: A ResNet basic block with two 3x3 convolutions and a shortcut branch that is either the identity or a 1x1 projection. In forward, the shortcut output is combined with the residual branch and the result passes through the final activation.
code:
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class BasicBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, stride=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(
            in_channels, out_channels,
            kernel_size=3, stride=stride, padding=1, bias=False
        )
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(
            out_channels, out_channels,
            kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False
        )
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)

        if stride != 1 or in_channels != out_channels:
            self.shortcut = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Conv2d(
                    in_channels, out_channels,
                    kernel_size=1, stride=stride, bias=False
                ),
                nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels),
            )
        else:
            self.shortcut = nn.Identity()

    def forward(self, x):
        # x: (N, in_channels, H, W)
        out = F.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)), inplace=True)
        out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out))
        out = <<BLANK:add>>
        <<BLANK:act>>
        return out
hints: The shortcut branch starts from the block input x, not from the intermediate value out.
The two paths are combined first; only then does the nonlinearity act on the sum.
explanation: The residual connection adds the shortcut of the original input to the output of the second batch norm: out + self.shortcut(x); the shortcut is the identity or a 1x1 conv + BN that matches the shape. The ReLU follows the addition: out = F.relu(out, inplace=True). Applying ReLU before the addition would prevent the residual branch from producing negative corrections and changes the architecture, and using self.shortcut(out) would project the wrong tensor instead of the block input. Assigning the ReLU result back to out matters because F.relu without assignment (and without inplace) would be discarded.

title: Scores and weights in a self-attention forward pass
description: A single-head self-attention layer: queries, keys and values come from one fused projection. The code computes the scaled similarity of every query with every key and turns each query's similarities into weights that are used to mix the values.
code:
import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class SelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(dim, 3 * dim)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(dim, dim)

    def forward(self, tokens):
        # tokens: (N, P, D)
        N, P, D = tokens.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(tokens).chunk(3, dim=-1)    # each (N, P, D)
        scores = <<BLANK:scores>>    # (N, P, P)
        attention = <<BLANK:weights>>    # (N, P, P)
        out = attention @ v    # (N, P, D)
        return self.proj(out)
hints: The scores of all (query, key) pairs form a (P, P) matrix per image. Which transposition of k makes the matrix product give that shape?
Dot products grow with the dimension D, so they are rescaled; and each query's weights should form a distribution over the keys. Which axis of (N, P, P) indexes the keys?
explanation: scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(D) multiplies (N, P, D) by (N, D, P) to get all query-key dot products, (N, P, P); the division by sqrt(D) keeps their variance near 1 so the softmax does not saturate. attention = scores.softmax(dim=-1) normalizes over the last axis, the keys, so every row (one query) sums to 1 and out = attention @ v is a convex combination of the values. Softmax over dim=1 would normalize over the queries instead, so rows would not sum to 1; omitting the sqrt(D) makes the softmax peaky and the gradients vanishing for large D.

title: Batch statistics versus per-sample statistics
prompt: Compare batch normalization and layer normalization: over which elements are the mean and variance computed, and what consequences does this have for small batch sizes and for the behaviour of the layer at test time?
model_answer: BatchNorm computes its mean and variance per channel over the batch (and spatial positions), so the output for a sample depends on the other samples in the batch. This makes the statistics noisy for small batches, and at test time it must switch to running averages collected during training. LayerNorm computes the statistics over the features of a single sample, so it does not depend on the batch, works with a batch of 1 and uses the same computation in training and evaluation.
key_points: BatchNorm normalizes over the batch (and spatial) dimension per channel; LayerNorm over the features of one sample.
BatchNorm becomes unreliable with small batches because the batch statistics are noisy.
BatchNorm needs running mean/variance (exponential moving averages) at test time, so train and eval modes differ.
LayerNorm needs no batch or running statistics and behaves identically in training and evaluation.
hints: What does a sample's normalized value depend on in each case?
What would you do at test time if you have a single example?
explanation: The key distinction is the axis of normalization: BatchNorm shares statistics across samples, LayerNorm does not. Everything else follows: batch dependence, sensitivity to batch size and the need for running estimates. Common half-answers only say that both normalize to zero mean and unit variance, or claim that LayerNorm has no learnable parameters; both still learn a per-feature gamma and beta.

source.item: Extra concept: attention scaling and softmax axis

title: Scaling and softmax direction in attention
prompt: In scaled dot-product self-attention the scores $QK^\top$ are divided by $\sqrt{D}$ and the softmax is taken over each row. Explain why the scaling is needed and what goes wrong if the softmax is taken over the columns instead.
model_answer: If the components of a query and a key are roughly independent with unit variance, their dot product has variance D, so scores grow with the dimension. Large scores push the softmax into a saturated, almost one-hot regime with tiny gradients, and dividing by sqrt(D) restores a variance of about 1. Row-wise softmax normalizes over the keys, so each query gets a probability distribution and its output is a convex combination of the values. Taking it over the columns would normalize over the queries, so the rows of the weights would no longer sum to 1 and the outputs would not be proper weighted averages.
key_points: Dot products of D-dimensional vectors have variance about D, so scores grow with D.
Large scores saturate the softmax and give vanishing gradients; dividing by sqrt(D) keeps the variance near 1.
Row-wise softmax is over the keys: each query gets weights that sum to 1 (a convex combination of the values).
A column-wise softmax normalizes over queries, so the output is not a weighted average of the values.
hints: How does the variance of a sum of D products of unit-variance terms scale with D?
Which index of A should sum to 1 so that Y = AV is an average of the rows of V?
explanation: The sqrt(D) factor is a variance correction that keeps the softmax in a regime with useful gradients. The softmax axis decides what the weights mean: one distribution over the keys per query. Typical mistakes are to say the scaling is only for numerical overflow, or to describe the softmax direction without saying what each normalization would mean for the output.

title: Order of tokens in self-attention
prompt: Explain why self-attention without positional encoding is permutation equivariant, and what practical problem this creates for tasks in which the order of the tokens matters.
model_answer: Every output is a weighted sum of value vectors, and the weights come only from pairwise dot products between queries and keys that are computed identically for every token. Reordering the inputs just reorders the rows and columns of the attention matrix and the rows of the output in the same way, so f(s(x)) = s(f(x)). The layer therefore cannot tell where a token is in the sequence (or image), and a shuffled input is treated like the original. Positional encodings or learned position embeddings must be added to the tokens to inject order information.
key_points: Queries, keys and values are computed per token with shared weights, and the weights depend only on pairwise similarities.
Permuting the inputs permutes the outputs in the same way: f(s(x)) = s(f(x)).
The layer cannot know the position of a token, so order and spatial layout are invisible.
Positional encodings or embeddings are added to the tokens to supply this information.
hints: What happens to the entries of A and Y if you swap two input rows?
If the model cannot see positions, what has to be added to the input?
explanation: Equivariance follows from the fact that nothing in the attention formula refers to the index of a token, only to its content. This is useful for sets but harmful for sequences and images. A common mistake is to say the output is invariant to the order (f(s(x)) = f(x)); the outputs are permuted, not unchanged.

source.item: Extra concept: pre-norm and zero initialisation

title: Where the normalization sits in a transformer block
prompt: A transformer block can place LayerNorm before each sub-layer (pre-norm) or after each residual addition (post-norm). Explain how the position affects the residual path, and why zero-initialising the last layer of each sub-layer gives an exact identity block only in the pre-norm variant.
model_answer: In the pre-norm block x = x + attn(norm1(x)), LayerNorm only acts on the input of each sub-layer, so the residual path from input to output stays untouched. In the post-norm block x = norm(x + attn(x)), the normalization is applied to the sum and therefore sits on the residual path. If the last linear layer of each sub-layer is zero-initialised, both sub-layers output exactly 0, so the pre-norm block returns x + 0 + 0 = x. The post-norm block still returns norm2(norm1(x)), which re-normalizes each token and is not the identity.
key_points: Pre-norm puts LayerNorm inside the residual branches; post-norm applies it to the sum x + sublayer(x).
In pre-norm the skip path from input to output contains no normalization.
With zero final weights and biases the sub-layers output 0, so the pre-norm block returns x unchanged.
Post-norm still applies the LayerNorms and returns norm2(norm1(x)), which is not x.
hints: Write both blocks as formulas and replace attn(.) and mlp(.) by 0.
Is norm1(x) equal to x for a general token x?
explanation: Zero-initialising the output layers makes each sub-layer contribute nothing at the start. In pre-norm this leaves only the clean skip connection, so the block starts as the identity; in post-norm the LayerNorms sit on the skip path and keep modifying x. A typical half-answer says that LayerNorm is always the identity at initialisation, which is false: it rescales every token to zero mean and unit variance.

source.item: Extra concept: residual block addition before ReLU

title: Why add the shortcut before the final activation
prompt: In a ResNet basic block the output is computed as ReLU(BN(conv(...)) + shortcut(x)). Explain the purpose of the shortcut, why it needs a 1x1 convolution in some blocks, and why the addition happens before the final ReLU.
model_answer: The shortcut lets the block learn a residual correction to its input and gives gradients a direct path around the convolutions, which makes deep networks easier to optimize. If the stride is not 1 or the number of channels changes, x and the residual branch have different shapes, so a 1x1 convolution (with the same stride) projects x to the right shape; otherwise an identity is used. The addition is placed before the ReLU so that the sum of both paths is passed through the nonlinearity and the residual branch can output negative corrections; applying the ReLU first would restrict the residual to non-negative values.
key_points: The shortcut gives a direct gradient path and lets the block learn a residual correction to its input.
A 1x1 convolution (with the block's stride) matches the shape of x when stride or channel count changes; otherwise identity.
The addition is done before the final ReLU, so the combined signal is activated.
Applying ReLU before the addition would force the residual to be non-negative and weaken its ability to correct x.
hints: What shapes must two tensors have to be added?
If the residual branch were passed through ReLU before the addition, what values could it contribute?
explanation: The shortcut makes the block compute x + F(x) instead of F(x), so depth does not prevent identity behaviour and gradients flow through the addition. The projection shortcut exists only for shape compatibility. Typical mistakes are to claim the 1x1 convolution adds capacity as the main purpose, or to forget that the final ReLU acts on the sum of both branches.
